name: Urapmin
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Only anthropological literature (Robbins) surfaced; no linguistic description of stress located

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is predictable by the following rules: Primary stress occurs on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel. In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is closed by a consonant, primary stress occurs on the final syllable. In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is open, primary stress occurs on the initial syllable. The above rules apply to the stems of inflected words.
new_statements.citation: Steinkraus, Walter. 1969. Tifal phonology showing vowel and tone neutralization. Kivung 2(1): 57-66.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable, not contrastive. The first long-vowel syllable of the word takes primary stress; if every vowel is short, stress goes to the final syllable when it is closed (CVC) and to the initial syllable when the final syllable is open. Inflected words stress their stem by the same rules (Boush 1994: on the final syllable of a simple verb stem). Vowel length is the weight criterion; coda weight only decides the all-short case.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress occurs on the second syllable with a lengthened vowel. In inflected words with more than three syllables in which all vowels are short, secondary stress occurs on the antepenult. No secondary stress occurs in words of three or less syllables in which all vowels are short.' (p. 64)
new_statements.exceptions: Non-inflected words of more than three syllables with all short vowels: 'extremely rare, and stress rules have not yet been posited for them.' No secondary stress in all-short words of three or fewer syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: rules are stated for non-inflected words of two or three syllables and for the stems of inflected words; longer uninflected all-short words 'extremely rare, and stress rules have not yet been posited for them'. Tifal also has two tonemes (high/low, one per syllable, §6 p. 63-64), so stress is a predictable, non-contrastive prominence alongside lexical tone. Steinkraus's data are from Tifalmin proper (Okbilabip, Ilam valley; fn. 1), not from Urapmin villages. The Boush 1994 Tifal OPD (p. 3), which explicitly lists Urapmin as a Tifal village, gives the same rule in short form and adds 'On inflected words primary stress occurs on the final syllable of a simple verb stem.' Contrast: Healey 1964 ch. IV §7.3 found no consistent loudness differences in Telefol, the language on Urapmin's other side.
new_statements.identity_note: No source describes Urapmin as such. The quoted statement is for Tifal [tif] (Glottolog tifa1245), Tifalmin dialect (Okbilabip). Healey 1964: 40-41 treats the Urapmin as a Tifal-speaking clan forming the 'Tifalmin-Urapmin' dialect group of Tifal, and the Boush 1994 Tifal OPD lists Urapmin among the Tifal 'major villages' and cites Urapmin-specific segmental features (initial /l/, /kw/) while giving the same stress rule; Wikipedia likewise lists Urap(min) as a Tifal dialect. Ethnologue/ISO separated Urapmin [urm] as 'geographically and linguistically between Tifal [tif] and Telefol [tlf]'. Telefol (tele1256; Healey 1964 ch. IV §7.3) is reported to have no detectable stress, so the Tifal rule should be filed for Urapmin only as a dialect-group proxy, flagged as such.

sources.note: §6 Tonemes (pp. 63-64): two tonemes, high and low, one per syllable, tone neutralized on word-initial short syllables. §7 Stress (p. 64): primary stress predictable — on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel; if all vowels short, on the final syllable when it is closed, on the initial syllable when it is open (words of 2-3 syllables; rules apply to stems of inflected words); secondary stress on the second long-vowel syllable, or on the antepenult in inflected all-short words of >3 syllables. sources.note: p. 3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'Stress is predictable. It occurs on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel, or on the final syllable of [sic: if] all the vowels are short and the final syllable is closed. If the final syllable is open, primary stress occurs on the initial syllable. On inflected words primary stress occurs on the final syllable of a simple verb stem.' Nothing on tone despite the heading. p. 1 lists 'Major villages: Tumobil, Busulmin, Bufumin, Okbilabip, Urapmin'; p. 3: 'Initial /l/ occurs only in Bufumin, Okbilabip, Yukubil, and Urapmin.
